justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a slight upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 14.1 is anchored heavily to the most recent observed price or level, assuming mean-reversion dynamics and minimal overnight drift. The one-week estimate nudges up marginally to 14.15, reflecting a modest positive bias that could stem from underlying trend momentum or slight fundamental tailwinds. The one-month estimate of 14.3 drifts a bit further in the same direction, incorporating a longer-run view that conditions remain broadly supportive, though the drift is deliberately modest given the inherent difficulty of forecasting over that horizon.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which is standard for time-series uncertainty that compounds over time. At one day, the interval of 13.65 to 14.55 is relatively tight because short-term volatility is relatively predictable and mean-reversion dampens extremes. By one week, the interval widens to 13.2–15.1, reflecting the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of trend changes that become more meaningful over several sessions. At one month, the interval expands considerably to 12.5–16.1, capturing the realistic range of outcomes when macroeconomic data releases, policy decisions, and sentiment shifts can all play a role. The asymmetry is roughly symmetric around the point estimate in each case, suggesting no strong directional skew was assumed.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, or a geopolitical shock could easily breach the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, stronger-than-expected demand data, a dovish policy surprise, or a short-covering rally could push the level above 16.1 within a month. Liquidity events or fat-tail market dislocations — things like a flash crash or a coordinated institutional move — represent tail risks that are structurally difficult to price into a standard confidence interval and represent the most likely way these bounds would be violated in practice.
